content: 1. Medications for Palliative Care: Dimenhydrinate, available in oral and injectable forms, is used to manage nausea and vomiting. Fluconazole, available in oral and injectable forms, is an antifungal medication. Fluoxetine, an oral selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI), is used to treat depression and anxiety. Furosemide, an oral diuretic, is used to manage fluid retention and edema. Haloperidol, available in oral and injectable forms, is used for agitation, delirium, and nausea. Hyoscine butylbromide, available in oral and injectable forms, is used to relieve abdominal cramping and spasms. Ibuprofen and related nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like naproxen, diclofenac, and meloxicam are used for pain and inflammation. Lactulose, sorbitol, or polyethylene glycol, all oral medications, are used to treat constipation. Loperamide, an oral medication, is used to manage diarrhea. Metoclopramide, an oral medication, is used to treat nausea and vomiting. Metronidazole, available in oral and injectable forms, can be crushed for topical use to manage infected wounds. Morphine, in oral immediate-release and injectable forms, is essential for managing moderate to severe pain and terminal dyspnea. Naloxone, an injectable medication, is used to reverse opioid overdoses. Omeprazole, an oral proton pump inhibitor, is used to manage acid reflux and gastrointestinal ulcers. Ondansetron, available in oral and injectable forms, is used to treat nausea and vomiting. Paracetamol (acetaminophen), an oral medication, is used for mild to moderate pain and fever. 2. Essential Equipment: Nasogastric tubes are used for patients with refractory vomiting or for administering medications and fluids. Urinary catheters are used to manage bladder dysfunction or outlet obstruction. Pressure-reducing mattresses (foam, water, or air) are essential for preventing and relieving pressure ulcers and associated pain. Locked safeboxes for opioids ensure secure storage to prevent misuse or theft. Flashlights with rechargeable batteries are necessary for nocturnal home care in areas without electricity. Adult diapers or improvised options using cotton and plastic are used to reduce the risk of skin ulceration and infection, as well as to ease caregiver burden. 3. Human Resources and Training: Doctors, nurses, and community health workers (CHWs) should receive basic training in palliative care to address physical and psychological suffering effectively. Training should include the diagnosis and management of pain, anxiety, depression, and delirium, as well as the safe prescription of opioids like morphine. CHWs can play a critical role in palliative care by providing emotional support, recognizing uncontrolled symptoms, and reporting findings to supervising clinicians. Family caregivers should be trained and equipped to provide basic nursing care, such as wound and mouth care, and medication administration. 4. Psychological and Social Support: Psychological suffering, including anxiety, depression, and grief, should be addressed through pharmacological and non-specialized psychological support. Social supports, such as food, housing, and transportation to medical care, are essential for patients and caregivers living in extreme poverty. Spiritual counseling should be offered to patients with serious or life-limiting conditions, tailored to their beliefs and needs. 5. Opioid Use and Safety: Morphine, in both oral and injectable forms, is the cornerstone of palliative care for managing moderate to severe pain and terminal dyspnea. Physicians should be trained to prescribe morphine safely and effectively, avoiding its use for mild pain or chronic non-malignant pain unless under special circumstances. Secure storage and record-keeping of opioids are critical to prevent diversion and misuse. In areas with high crime rates, additional precautions may be necessary to ensure safe access to opioids without placing patients or families at risk. 6. Specialized Medications: Haloperidol is a first-line treatment for nausea, vomiting, agitation, delirium, and anxiety. Fluoxetine is the first-line pharmacotherapy for depression and persistent anxiety, common in humanitarian emergencies. Petroleum jelly is essential for dressing non-healable wounds and preventing pain or bleeding during dressing changes. Metronidazole powder, made by crushing tablets, is used to reduce odor from wounds infected with anaerobic bacteria. 7. Integration of Palliative Care in Humanitarian Crises: Palliative care should be integrated into responses to humanitarian emergencies to address the needs of patients with serious, complex, or life-limiting conditions. Clinicians should use available resources, including telemedicine, to provide the best possible care under challenging circumstances. CHWs can provide critical support by visiting patients frequently, recognizing symptoms, and ensuring comfort. 8. Training and Capacity Building: Basic palliative care training should be provided to local clinicians during prolonged health crises to improve access to care and strengthen local healthcare capacity. Training should include the management of mental, neurological, and substance use disorders, as outlined in WHO guidelines.
